readings.title: How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin
readings.challenge: Follow a rude act and its delayed revenge, and enjoy a long phrase that keeps coming back.
readings.focus: A small, patient cook gets even with a huge, rude animal.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. A Superior Comestible is a very fine thing to eat; a sloka is a verse in an old Indian form; a waterproof is a raincoat; the P. and O. was a line of passenger steamships. The places at the end are real and made-up names mixed together.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Parsee is a member of the Parsi community of India, whose ancestors came from Persia; Kipling draws him as a comic figure, and “more-than-oriental splendour” uses an old word for the lands of Asia. These belong to Kipling’s time.

excerpt.locator: “How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin,” the whole story with its closing verse; opens “ONCE upon a time, on an uninhabited island on the shores of the Red Sea, there lived a…”; closes “…Suez For the likes of you and me Ever to go In a P. and O. And call on the Cake-Parsee!”.

questions.prompt: What did the Rhinoceros do to the Parsee’s cake? What does the narrator say about his manners?
facilitatorNotes: He knocked over the stove, spiked the cake on his horn and ate it. He “had no manners then, and he has no manners now, and he never will have any manners”: the narrator says it as if it were a law of nature.
evidence: he spiked that cake on the horn of his nose, and he ate it,
he had no manners then, and he has no manners now, and he never will have any manners.

questions.prompt: How was the Rhinoceros’s skin different in those days?
facilitatorNotes: It fitted tight with no wrinkles, buttoned underneath with three buttons, and could be taken off like a raincoat.
evidence: In those days it buttoned underneath with three buttons and looked like a waterproof.

questions.prompt: How did the Parsee get even? Why didn’t he simply fight the Rhinoceros?
facilitatorNotes: He filled the skin with stale, tickly cake-crumbs and burned currants while the Rhinoceros bathed, then waited up his palm tree. He is far smaller than the Rhinoceros; he wins by patience and a trick.
evidence: he rubbed that skin just as full of old, dry, stale, tickly cake-crumbs and some burned currants as ever it could possibly hold.

questions.prompt: After the Parsee’s rhyme, the narrator says “there was a great deal more in that than you would think.” What was the “more”?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme was a warning that came true: taking the cake led to the crumbs, the folds and the bad temper that, the story says, every rhinoceros has to this day. Readers may also say the rhyme sounds like a curse.
evidence: And there was a great deal more in that than you would think.
from that day to this every rhinoceros has great folds in his skin and a very bad temper,

questions.prompt: Kipling repeats “from whose hat the rays of the sun were reflected in more-than-oriental splendour.” Why might a storyteller keep repeating a long phrase?
facilitatorNotes: It is fun to say aloud, it makes the Parsee easy to picture, and listeners start to wait for it. In a story meant to be told “just so,” the repeats are part of the music. Some listeners find it funnier each time.
evidence: from whose hat the rays of the sun were reflected in more-than-oriental splendour.

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — ’satiable curtiosity (part 1)
readings.challenge: Enjoy the repeated phrases, and notice what happens every single time the Elephant’s Child asks a question.
readings.focus: A young elephant’s curiosity is punished again and again, yet sends him on a long journey.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. Long ago, this story says, elephants had no trunks. “’Satiable curtiosity” is the narrator’s way of saying insatiable curiosity, a curiosity that is never satisfied. “Dretful” means dreadful; “promiscuous parts” here means “all sorts of places around here.” Graham’s Town, Kimberley and Khama’s Country are places in southern Africa.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The young elephant is spanked by every relative he questions; spanking was a common punishment in Kipling’s time.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from the beginning through his meeting with the Python, ending “what he thought was a log of wood”; opens “IN the High and Far-Off Times the Elephant, O Best Beloved, had no trunk. He had only a…”; closes “…very edge of the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Elephant’s Child do with his “’satiable curtiosity,” and what happens each time?
facilitatorNotes: He asks question after question about everything, and every relative spanks him for it. “And still he was full of ’satiable curtiosity!” repeats like a chorus.
evidence: he asked ever so many questions.
and all his uncles and his aunts spanked him.

questions.prompt: Which question brings the biggest spanking of all? Why might everyone say “Hush!”?
facilitatorNotes: “What does the Crocodile have for dinner?” They may be afraid of the Crocodile, or of the answer, since a crocodile might eat a young elephant. The story lets readers guess.
evidence: What does the Crocodile have for dinner?
Then everybody said, 'Hush!' in a loud and dretful tone,

questions.prompt: Find the long phrase Kipling repeats about the river. Why do you think he repeats it?
facilitatorNotes: “The great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees.” It sounds like a chant, is fun to say together, and makes the place feel far away and important.
evidence: the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees,

questions.prompt: The part ends when he treads on “what he thought was a log of wood.” What do you predict, and which clue earlier in the story points to it?
facilitatorNotes: It is probably the Crocodile: the narrator has told us he “had never seen a Crocodile, and did not know what one was like,” so he would not recognize one.
evidence: this 'satiable Elephant's Child had never seen a Crocodile, and did not know what one was like.
till he trod on what he thought was a log of wood

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — the tug-of-war (part 2)
readings.challenge: Read the funny voices aloud, and work out what the long, grand names really mean.
readings.focus: Curiosity nearly costs the Elephant’s Child everything, and leaves him with something new.
readings.context: Recap: the Elephant’s Child, who is spanked for every question he asks, has travelled to the Limpopo River to find out what the Crocodile has for dinner. A python has spanked him too. Now he has stepped on what he thought was a log. Crocodile tears are pretend tears; an ulster is a long overcoat; a man-of-war is a warship; to vitiate is to spoil; “hijjus” means hideous, terribly.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Crocodile tries to eat the Elephant’s Child and stretches his nose painfully.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from “But it was really the Crocodile” through the three days’ wait, ending “same as all Elephants have to-day”; opens “But it was really the Crocodile, O Best Beloved, and the Crocodile winked one eye—like…”; closes “…Crocodile had pulled it out into a really truly trunk same as all Elephants have to-day.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Crocodile prove who he is? What is odd about that proof?
facilitatorNotes: He weeps crocodile tears “to show it was quite true.” Crocodile tears are fake tears, so his proof is really a warning sign. Listeners may spot the danger before the Elephant’s Child does.
evidence: he wept crocodile-tears to show it was quite true.

questions.prompt: Why does the Elephant’s Child say, “Led go! You are hurtig be!” Read it aloud the way he would.
facilitatorNotes: The Crocodile is holding his nose, so his words come out blocked: “Let go! You are hurting me!” Holding one’s own nose and saying it shows how Kipling spelled the sound.
evidence: 'Led go! You are hurtig be!'

questions.prompt: The Python calls the Crocodile two grand names. What are they, and why do they fit?
facilitatorNotes: “Your acquaintance in the large-pattern leather ulster”: his scaly hide looks like a big leather coat. “Self-propelling man-of-war with the armour-plated upper deck”: he is huge, armored and moves through water like a warship. The Python never says anything simply.
evidence: your acquaintance in the large-pattern leather ulster
yonder self-propelling man-of-war with the armour-plated upper deck

questions.prompt: The Elephant’s Child waits for his nose to shrink, and the Python says, “Some people do not know what is good for them.” What does the Python know that the Elephant’s Child does not yet know?
facilitatorNotes: That the stretched nose is not a disaster: it is a useful trunk, “same as all Elephants have to-day.” Some readers may feel sorry for him first; both feelings fit.
evidence: Some people do not know what is good for them.
the Crocodile had pulled it out into a really truly trunk same as all Elephants have to-day.

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — ’vantages, and the way home (part 3)
readings.challenge: List what a new trunk can do, then judge what the Elephant’s Child does with it.
readings.focus: A painful accident turns out to be useful, and the Elephant’s Child goes home to settle the score.
readings.context: Recap: the Crocodile caught the curious Elephant’s Child by his small nose and pulled until, with the Python’s help, he got free; but his nose has stretched into a long trunk. He has waited three days for it to shrink. To hove is to throw; a pachyderm is a thick-skinned animal such as an elephant; a fly-whisk is a brush for flicking away flies.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Elephant’s Child gets revenge by spanking and roughly treating his whole family.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from the fly on the third day to the end of the story, with the verse “I keep six honest serving-men”; opens “At the end of the third day a fly came and stung him on the shoulder, and before he knew…”; closes “…second she opens her eyes— One million Hows, two million Wheres, And seven million Whys!”.

questions.prompt: What three “’vantages” does the Python point out? Why couldn’t the Elephant’s Child do these with his old nose?
facilitatorNotes: Swatting a fly, plucking grass to eat, and slapping a cool mud-cap on his head. His old “mere-smear nose” could not reach or grip anything.
evidence: 'Vantage number one!' said the Bi-Coloured-Python-Rock-Snake.
he schlooped up a schloop of mud from the banks of the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo,

questions.prompt: What does he do on the way home that makes him a “Tidy Pachyderm”?
facilitatorNotes: He picks up all the melon rinds he dropped on the way to the river, when he had no way to pick them up.
evidence: he picked up the melon rinds that he had dropped on his way to the Limpopo—for he was a Tidy Pachyderm.

questions.prompt: When his family wants to spank him again, what does he do? Is it fair, or has he become just as bad as they were?
facilitatorNotes: He spanks them all, throws the Baboon into a hornets’ nest and pulls the Ostrich’s feathers, but never lets anyone touch the Kolokolo Bird, who helped him. The narrator calls him “that bad Elephant’s Child,” yet in the end “nobody spanked anybody any more.” Readers may argue it is fair payback, or that he has turned into a bully.
evidence: Then that bad Elephant's Child spanked all his dear families for a long time,
but he never let any one touch Kolokolo Bird.

questions.prompt: The verse at the end names “six honest serving-men.” Who are they really, and who is the “person small” who keeps ten million?
facilitatorNotes: They are the question words: What, Where, When, How, Why and Who. (This printing repeats “Where” in the fourth line, where most printings have “Why.”) The person small is a curious child who never stops asking, much like the Elephant’s Child; Kipling may mean his own daughter.
evidence: I keep six honest serving-men;
One million Hows, two million Wheres,

readings.title: The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo
readings.challenge: Listen for a wish that grows, a chase that repeats, and a short line that answers every change.
readings.focus: A proud animal gets exactly what he asked for, in a way he did not expect.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. The adult reads this one aloud; the child can join in on “He had to!” Inordinate means far too much; spinifex, mulga, blue gums and ti-trees are Australian plants; a salt-pan is a dried-up salty lake; a dingo is an Australian wild dog. “Played Old Scratch with” means ruined.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. Nqa, Nquing and Nqong are gods Kipling invented for the story; they are not the beliefs of Aboriginal Australians.

excerpt.locator: “The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo,” the whole story with its closing verse; opens “NOT always was the Kangaroo as now we do behold him, but a Different Animal with four…”; closes “…But your legs would develop terrific— Yes, my importunate son, You'd be a Marvellous Kid!”.

questions.prompt: What did Kangaroo ask each of the three gods? How does his wish grow each time?
facilitatorNotes: Nqa: make me different from all other animals by five o’clock. Nquing: different, and wonderfully popular. Nqong: different, popular and “wonderfully run after.” Each time he asks for more.
evidence: Make me different from all other animals by five this afternoon.
make me popular and wonderfully run after by five this afternoon.

questions.prompt: How does Nqong grant the wish? Why is it a trick?
facilitatorNotes: He sends Dingo to chase Kangaroo: “run after” comes true word for word. Kangaroo meant admired; Nqong takes it literally.
evidence: He wants to be popular and very truly run after. Dingo, make him so!

questions.prompt: What short line keeps answering the story, and what does it mean each time?
facilitatorNotes: “He had to!” Kangaroo has no choice: the chase forces every change, from aching legs to hopping on two. Read it together each time it comes.
evidence: He had to!

questions.prompt: At the end, Kangaroo and Dingo each say, “That’s your fault.” Whose fault is it, in your view?
facilitatorNotes: Kangaroo asked for it, as Nqong reminds him; Nqong chose a hard way to grant it; Dingo only did as he was told and still has no dinner. Readers can blame different characters if they give a reason from the story.
evidence: didn't you ask me to make you different from all other animals, as well as to make you very truly sought after?
each said, 'That's your fault.'

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — which is which? (part 1)
readings.challenge: Untangle sentences that are tangled on purpose, and keep track of who is who.
readings.focus: Two small animals defend themselves by confusing a hungry jaguar with words.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. Turbid means muddy; the Amazon is the great river of South America; a jaguar is a big spotted cat. “To save my spots” is the Jaguar’s way of saying “for the life of me.”
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from the beginning through the Jaguar’s paw full of prickles; opens “THIS, O Best Beloved, is another story of the High and Far-Off Times. In the very middle…”; closes “…scratched his head with his un-prickly paw—'how do I know that this other is Tortoise?'”.

questions.prompt: What did Mother Jaguar tell her son about catching hedgehogs and tortoises?
facilitatorNotes: Drop a hedgehog into the water so it uncoils; scoop a tortoise out of its shell with your paw. Her advice only works if he can tell them apart.
evidence: when you find a Hedgehog you must drop him into the water and then he will uncoil,
when you catch a Tortoise you must scoop him out of his shell with your paw.

questions.prompt: Why can’t Painted Jaguar tell which animal is which?
facilitatorNotes: Both have hidden themselves: one curled into a ball, the other drew into its shell. He admits, “I can’t tell.”
evidence: Now which of you is Hedgehog and which is Tortoise? because to save my spots, I can't tell.

questions.prompt: How do Stickly-Prickly and Slow-Solid confuse the Jaguar? Try reading one of their versions of his mother’s advice aloud.
facilitatorNotes: They scramble the words of her advice into nonsense, so he begins to doubt what he remembers. Reading it aloud shows how tangled it is.
evidence: Perhaps she said that when you uncoil a Tortoise you must shell him out of the water with a scoop,

questions.prompt: Stickly-Prickly says, “you can scoop me out of my shell if you like.” Why is that a clever trick, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: It makes the Jaguar think he must be the Tortoise, so he grabs with his paw and gets a pawful of prickles; Stickly-Prickly is knocked away into the dark. The Jaguar learns which one he is not, but still cannot be sure about the other.
evidence: 'Aha!' said Painted Jaguar. 'Now I know you're Tortoise.
Jaguar's paddy-paw was just filled with prickles.

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — the truthful Tortoise (part 2)
readings.challenge: Follow a character who tells the truth in a way that makes it hard to believe.
readings.focus: The Tortoise escapes by telling the truth, but Mother Jaguar gives her son a rule he cannot forget.
readings.context: Recap: Painted Jaguar wants to eat Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog and Slow-Solid Tortoise, but cannot tell which is which. They tangled up his mother’s advice, and when he grabbed the one he thought was Tortoise, he got a paw full of prickles. Now he turns to Slow-Solid. To be “mixy” is the Jaguar’s word for muddled.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from “But I am Tortoise” through the Jaguar’s rhyme; opens “'But I am Tortoise,' said Slow-and-Solid. 'Your mother was quite right. She said that you…”; closes “…can swim— Slow-Solid, that's him! Curls up, but can't swim— Stickly-Prickly, that's him!'”.

questions.prompt: Slow-and-Solid tells the Jaguar how to make him swim away. Why doesn’t the Jaguar believe him?
facilitatorNotes: He is so muddled that he decides the opposite of whatever the Tortoise wants must be right: “as you seem so anxious to be dropped I think you don’t want to be dropped.” So he does exactly what lets the Tortoise escape.
evidence: if you want to see me swim away you've only got to drop me into the water.
as you seem so anxious to be dropped I think you don't want to be dropped.

questions.prompt: Read aloud the speech beginning “Well, suppose you say that I said that she said.” What is the Tortoise trying to do?
facilitatorNotes: Tie the Jaguar’s thinking in knots so that he gives up trusting his own memory. It works: the Jaguar says he does not know whether he is on his head or his tail.
evidence: if she said what you said I said she said, it's just the same as if I said what she said she said.

questions.prompt: Mother Jaguar gives new, clear rules. What are they, and why do they worry the two friends?
facilitatorNotes: A hedgehog curls into a ball with prickles; a tortoise cannot curl, only draw in. The rules are simple enough that “even Painted Jaguar can’t forget” them, so the friends’ tricks will not work again.
evidence: A Tortoise can't curl himself up,
Even Painted Jaguar can't forget those directions.

questions.prompt: Painted Jaguar turns his mother’s rules into a rhyme. Why might a rhyme help him? How could the two friends defeat it?
facilitatorNotes: Rhymes are easy to remember. The friends could only beat it by changing what they can do; readers may predict that each will learn the other’s trick.
evidence: Can't curl, but can swim— Slow-Solid, that's him!

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — practice in the river (part 3)
readings.challenge: Notice a word that keeps repeating, and spot the changes before the characters do.
readings.focus: Two friends teach each other their own skills, and their bodies begin to change.
readings.context: Recap: Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog and Slow-Solid Tortoise escaped Painted Jaguar by confusing him, but his mother taught him a rhyme: a tortoise can’t curl but can swim; a hedgehog curls up but can’t swim. Now the friends make a plan. A chestnut-burr is the prickly case of a chestnut; a side-stroke is a way of swimming.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from “He'll never forget that” through the friends’ plan to find the Jaguar; opens “'He'll never forget that this month of Sundays,' said Stickly-Prickly. 'Hold up my chin,…”; closes “…of being able to swim. Oh, won't Painted Jaguar be surprised! Let's go and find him.'”.

questions.prompt: What does each friend decide to learn, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Stickly-Prickly will learn to swim and Slow-Solid will learn to curl up, so the Jaguar’s rhyme will no longer tell them apart. “It may be useful,” they both say.
evidence: I'm going to try to learn to swim. It may be useful.
I'll see what I can do towards curling up. It may be useful.

questions.prompt: Find the word the friends keep saying to each other. What does it show about how they help each other?
facilitatorNotes: “Excellent!” Each praises the other’s small progress, holds up a chin or unlaces a plate. They are patient teachers.
evidence: 'Excellent!' said Slow-and-Solid;
You'll make a fine swimmer yet,

questions.prompt: How are their bodies changing as they practise? Find the clue about pine-cones.
facilitatorNotes: The Tortoise’s plates now overlap, and the Hedgehog’s prickles are melting together so he looks like a pine-cone instead of a chestnut-burr. They are becoming alike.
evidence: They are all overlapping now, instead of lying side by side.
you're growing to look rather more like a pine-cone, and less like a chestnut-burr,

questions.prompt: Each friend says the other’s hard trick is “so easy.” Is it? Why might they say so?
facilitatorNotes: It is not easy: the Tortoise strains until he goes “black in the face” and grunts. Saying “so easy” may be encouragement, or friendly teasing; readers can decide.
evidence: It's making you black in the face.
which you say is so easy.

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — two new animals (part 4)
readings.challenge: Find how a rhyme from earlier has been turned around, and judge a mother’s rule.
readings.focus: The friends turn the Jaguar’s rule against him, and become a new animal.
readings.context: Recap: to beat Painted Jaguar’s rhyme (“Can’t curl, but can swim, Slow-Solid, that’s him!”), Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog learned to swim and Slow-Solid Tortoise learned to curl. Practising all night, their prickles and plates turned into overlapping scales. Now they go to find the Jaguar. The Don and the Magdalena in the closing verse were steamships sailing from Southampton, England, to Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from the meeting with the Jaguar to the end of the story, with the verse “I've never sailed the Amazon”; opens “By and by they found Painted Jaguar, still nursing his paddy-paw that had been hurt the…”; closes “…to Rio— Roll really down to Rio! Oh, I'd love to roll to Rio Some day before I'm old!”.

questions.prompt: How does the Jaguar react when he sees them? Why doesn’t he recognize them?
facilitatorNotes: He is so astonished he falls backward over his tail three times. They no longer look like a hedgehog and a tortoise; both are scaly.
evidence: He was so astonished that he fell three times backward over his own painted tail without stopping.

questions.prompt: Stickly-Prickly recites the Jaguar’s own rhyme, with a change. What has changed, and why is it now true?
facilitatorNotes: The names have swapped: now Stickly-Prickly can swim and Slow-Solid can curl. The rhyme stayed the same; the animals changed.
evidence: Can't curl, but can swim— Stickly-Prickly, that's him!

questions.prompt: Mother Jaguar says “a Hedgehog is a Hedgehog, and can't be anything but a Hedgehog.” Is she right in this story?
facilitatorNotes: No: the friends changed by practice and help. But her other advice, to call it “Armadillo” and leave it alone, is wise. Readers can weigh which part of her answer is right.
evidence: a Hedgehog is a Hedgehog, and can't be anything but a Hedgehog;
And I should leave it alone.

questions.prompt: The narrator says they were called Armadillos “because they were so clever.” What was clever about what they did? What does the verse at the end wish for?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of hiding, each learned the other’s way of staying safe, and turned the Jaguar’s rule upside down. In the verse Kipling says he has never been to Brazil or seen a jaguar or an armadillo, and wishes he could sail to Rio before he is old.
evidence: are always called Armadillos, because they were so clever.
I've never seen a Jaguar,
